implementation_notes: The double class is generated at compile time from the abstract collaborator by the MOCK_METHOD macros, so the compiler still checks every signature; the test then configures it with ON_CALL(mock, method(args)).WillByDefault(Return(v)) for default answers and EXPECT_CALL(mock, method(args)).Times(n).WillOnce(Invoke(f)) / WillRepeatedly(Return(v)) / Throw(exc) for expectations and failures, with NiceMock/StrictMock choosing how uninteresting calls are treated. That replaces the hand-written configuration interface, and the generated class is the reusable double across tests.
pitfalls: Once EXPECT_CALL is used for a method, calls to it that match no expectation become errors, so a partial stub set turns an unimportant call into a failure.
The mocked methods must be virtual (and the destructor virtual); a non-virtual method is silently not intercepted.
MOCK_METHOD needs the mock class to be regenerated by hand when the interface changes, which is the C++ analogue of stale generated mocks.

variants.name: Injected std::function members configured with per-test lambdas
variants.idiom_name: collaborator injected as std::function members; per-test lambdas
variants.implementation_notes: When the collaboration is one call (or a handful), the double collapses into a small struct whose members are std::function objects; each test assigns a lambda that returns the canned value or throws, which is the configuration step, and std::function type-erases the callable so no double class is defined. This is the cheaper structure for narrow, functional seams; the class-based form is still justified when the collaborator interface is wide, when the test should be forced to answer every method, or when the double must also record calls.
pitfalls: std::function copies the callable: a lambda capturing by reference can outlive nothing once the test returns and dangles into the next test.
Calling an empty std::function throws std::bad_function_call instead of failing an assertion, so an unconfigured member should be given an explicit default that fails the test.
No argument checking happens unless the lambda performs it; the seam gives you control points, not expectations.
